what: The Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya and its three-doṣa medicine, translated into Tibetan (in the Tengyur); scholars trace much of the Four Tantras (rGyud bzhi) to it.

evidence.detail: Tibetan translation of the Aṣṭāṅgahṛdaya in the Tengyur (recalled)
The Tibetan tradition's own account has the Four Tantras taught by the Medicine Buddha; kept apart from the scholarly account

what: The three humours (vātam, pittam, kapam), the seven tissues and much Sanskrit medical vocabulary shared by Āyurveda and Siddha medicine.

evidence.detail: the Siddha tradition derives its medicine from Śiva through Agastya (see U22)

what: Doṣa vocabulary and the aim of balancing the doṣas used to frame the haṭha cleansing acts and breath practices (HYP 2.21).

evidence.detail: medas, śleṣman, doṣa, vāta-pitta-kapha in the Haṭhapradīpikā

what: The verse on mercury and breath ('swooned it removes disease, dead it revives, bound it gives sky-going') and the parallel of binding mercury and mind.

evidence.detail: the Rasārṇava is generally dated earlier than the Haṭhapradīpikā

what: The ten sinful acts of body, speech and mind (AHS Sū 2.21-22) and the homage to the 'unprecedented physician' who destroyed the diseases of passion (AHS Sū 1.1).

evidence.detail: AHS Sū 2.21-22 = the ten akuśala karmapathas

what: The eight causes of the non-perception of existing things (Ca Sū 11.8 ≈ Sāṃkhyakārikā 7).
Yoga as the cessation (here of feeling), the powers of yogins and the path of the recollection of truth shared by Caraka Śā 1 with Yoga and Sāṃkhya ('the yogins … the liberated Sāṃkhyas', Śā 1.151).

evidence.detail: Ca Śā 1.151 names the yogins and the Sāṃkhyas

what: The Kaula frame of the Rasārṇava — the Goddess addresses Bhairava as destroyer of the Kula, Kaula and Siddha-kaula; rasa does not succeed for those without the Kula teaching.
Mercurial and metallic medicines absorbed into the later Āyurvedic compendia (Śārṅgadhara, Bhāvaprakāśa, Yogaratnākara) and into Āyurvedic pharmacy.
Āyurveda recast for Jain ethics in Ugrāditya's Kalyāṇakāraka (no meat, alcohol or honey).
Nāth siddhas counted as rasa-siddhas and rasa authors (Carpaṭi, Nityanātha); the ideal of an immortal, perfected body shared.
